topic: Claude Opus 4 vs Sonnet 4: When to Use Each Model (2026)

key_points: Frames Opus 4 as the long-horizon, complex-reasoning choice and Sonnet 4 as the lower-cost daily development model.
Highlights the useful tension for buyers: Sonnet 4 can be close enough for many coding tasks, while Opus 4 wins when a task requires deeper planning or sustained autonomy.
Good competitor to outrank with a clearer 2026 migration note and a decision matrix for engineering teams.
Compares API usage, cost, context, and practical production tradeoffs.
Emphasizes the 5x token-price gap: Sonnet 4 at $3 input/$15 output per million tokens versus Opus 4 at $15/$75.
Concludes that Sonnet 4 is the better default for most high-volume applications unless premium reasoning is needed.
Developer-workflow angle focused on Claude Code, SWE-bench, Terminal-bench, tool use, and codebase navigation.
Positions Opus 4 as strongest for uninterrupted multi-step software work and Sonnet 4 as the balanced upgrade from Sonnet 3.7.
Useful benchmark-driven competitor, but it lacks an updated 2026 section on deprecation and newer Claude 4.x successors.
Hands-on evaluation style with writing, coding, and cost takeaways.
Argues Sonnet 4 delivers similar quality for routine writing and content tasks at a much lower cost.
A good model for practical examples; can be beaten by adding enterprise routing guidance and benchmark/stat citations.
Important 2026 freshness angle: original Claude Sonnet 4 and Opus 4 model IDs are scheduled for retirement on June 15, 2026.
Recommends Sonnet 4.5 as the default replacement for Sonnet 4 and Opus 4.5 or newer Opus releases for Opus 4 users.
This creates an opportunity to make the comparison article more current: when to use each model family, and when to migrate instead of choosing the original 4.0 IDs.

stats.fact: Anthropic launched Claude Opus 4 and Claude Sonnet 4 as hybrid models with near-instant and extended-thinking modes; at launch, Opus 4 cost $15 per million input tokens and $75 per million output tokens, while Sonnet 4 cost $3 and $15 respectively.
Anthropic described Claude Opus 4 as its strongest coding model at launch, reporting 72.5% on SWE-bench and 43.2% on Terminal-bench, with sustained performance for long-running tasks.
Claude Sonnet 4 was positioned as the more efficient general-purpose option; Anthropic made Sonnet 4 available to free Claude users, while Opus 4 required paid Claude plans.

The Claude API models overview now lists newer current models: Claude Opus 4.8 at $5 input/$25 output per million tokens and Claude Sonnet 4.6 at $3 input/$15 output per million tokens, both with 1M-token context windows in the listed comparison.
Anthropic's current model guidance says Opus-tier models are for complex reasoning, long-horizon agentic coding, and high-autonomy work, while Sonnet is the best speed/intelligence balance.

A 2026 migration guide reports that the original claude-sonnet-4-0 and claude-opus-4-0 identifiers are scheduled to stop working after June 15, 2026, making pinned API usage a near-term migration risk.

The Verge reported Anthropic's launch claim that both Claude 4 models were 65% less likely than Sonnet 3.7 to take shortcuts or exploit loopholes, and that Opus 4 had demonstrated several-hour autonomous runs in customer testing.

Business Insider reported in April 2026 that Anthropic updated Claude Code usage estimates to about $13 per enterprise developer per active day and $150-250 per developer per month, with 90% of users below $30 per active day.

angles: Lead with the practical answer: use Sonnet 4/Sonnet 4.x as the default for daily coding, chat, documentation, content, and high-volume workflows; escalate to Opus 4/Opus 4.x for architecture, complex debugging, agentic coding, research synthesis, and high-stakes reasoning.
Add a 2026 warning box: if the reader is literally choosing the original 4.0 API IDs, the better decision may be migration to Sonnet 4.6 or Opus 4.8 rather than a fresh 4.0 integration.

Explain cost by workflow rather than only token price: Opus can be 5x more expensive on original 4.0 pricing, but may reduce retries on hard tasks; Sonnet usually wins for throughput and predictable unit economics.
Use a routing strategy angle: start with Sonnet for drafts, routine code edits, tests, summaries, and customer-facing volume; route only failed, ambiguous, multi-file, or architectural tasks to Opus.
Differentiate from competitor posts by adding a developer decision matrix, sample model-router rules, and examples by task size: one prompt, one file, many files, multi-hour agent run.
Clarify that benchmark headlines can mislead: Sonnet may match or exceed Opus on some coding scores, but Opus is chosen for consistency under long context, hard constraints, and ambiguous goals.
Tie the comparison to Claude Code budgets: model choice is now an engineering cost-control decision, not just a quality preference.
